notes.title: Concept - Why Models Don't Fit on One GPU
notes.scope: The memory budget of training and why a modern LLM exceeds a single GPU's HBM, motivating sharding and parallelism. IN: the four memory consumers, the ~16-20 bytes/param rule, activation memory, the two axes (shard-the-model vs shard-the-states). OUT: the parallelism mechanisms themselves (own notes) and exact per-tensor memory formulas (link to 08 Reference - Memory Math for Transformers).
key_points: Four consumers of training memory: parameters (2 bytes bf16), gradients (2-4 bytes), optimizer states (Adam fp32 master + m + v = 12 bytes/param), and activations (batch x seq dependent). Adam mixed-precision totals ~16-20 bytes/param.
Concrete: a 7B model needs ~112-140 GB just for weights+grads+optimizer states, already exceeding an 80GB H100 before a single activation is stored; 70B is flatly impossible on one device.

Activation memory scales with batch x seq x layers x hidden and dominates at long context; gradient/activation checkpointing (recomputation) trades ~30% extra compute to drop activation memory to O(sqrt(layers)).

A single 80GB GPU caps trainable dense models near ~3-6B params without sharding; everything larger requires splitting either the tensors (TP/PP) or the redundant optimizer/param state across ranks (ZeRO/FSDP).
HBM capacity and bandwidth, not raw FLOPs, is usually the binding constraint — the memory wall, not the compute wall (foreshadows the roofline model).
Failure signatures: OOM at step 0 (static footprint too large) vs OOM after N steps (activation peak, optimizer-state lazy allocation, or allocator fragmentation) — different bugs, different fixes.

notes.title: Concept - Byte-Pair Encoding
notes.scope: The BPE algorithm as used to tokenize LLM training corpora: greedy merge training, encoding by merge rank, and byte-level BPE. IN: the merge procedure, byte-level guarantee, pre-tokenization, vocab/sequence-length numbers. OUT: unigram/SentencePiece and vocab-size decisions (link Concept - Tokenizer Training), inference-time arcana (link Gotchas - Tokenizers), glitch tokens (link 18 Lore - Glitch Tokens).
key_points: Training: start from bytes/characters, iteratively merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, and record the merge order; final vocab = base symbols + N learned merges. Encoding replays merges greedily in rank order.
Byte-level BPE (GPT-2; original BPE from Sennrich et al. 2016 / Gage 1994) operates over the 256 byte values so every possible string is encodable with no UNK token; GPT-2 vocab = 50257.

Pre-tokenization splits text with a regex (whitespace/punctuation) before merging so merges never cross word boundaries; GPT-2 marks leading spaces with the special glyph 'G-with-dot' rather than a literal space.

Numbers: typical vocab 32k-256k; English compresses to ~3.5-4 chars/token, code and non-English are worse; the embedding + unembedding matrix costs vocab x hidden params, coupling tokenizer choice to model size.
Failure modes: whitespace and digit merges cause arithmetic errors; multilingual text under-segments (high fertility); some byte sequences are not perfectly invertible under naive normalization.

Non-obvious: BPE merges are frequency-greedy, not likelihood-optimal (unlike unigram LM); the tokenizer is frozen before pretraining and silently shapes loss, context length, and every downstream capability.

notes.title: Concept - Gradient Accumulation and Microbatching
notes.scope: Splitting a large effective batch into microbatches whose gradients are summed before one optimizer step, to hit a target token batch on limited HBM. IN: the effective-batch formula, no_sync, the loss-normalization bug, interaction with clipping and loss scaling. OUT: pipeline scheduling of microbatches (link Concept - Tensor and Pipeline Parallelism), critical-batch theory (link Concept - Critical Batch Size).
key_points: Effective batch = microbatch_size x grad_accum_steps x data_parallel_world_size; this is how a run targets a fixed token budget per step (e.g., 4M tokens) despite per-GPU memory limits.

Mechanism: run forward/backward per microbatch accumulating into .grad, then one optimizer.step() per accumulation window; in DDP wrap all but the last microbatch in no_sync() so gradient all-reduce fires once, not per microbatch.

The 2024 loss-normalization bug (surfaced by Unsloth/HF): averaging per-microbatch mean losses when microbatches contain unequal token counts (from padding or packing) silently mis-weights the gradient; correct fix is to sum per-token losses and divide by the global token count.
Numbers: LLM pretraining batches span 0.5M-16M tokens; grad-accum of 4-64 is common; more accumulation means fewer DP syncs per token (comm-cheaper) at identical total compute.
Interaction with mixed precision and clipping: unscale the loss-scaled gradient before clipping, and clip on the fully accumulated global-norm gradient, not per microbatch.
Failure mode: forgetting the 1/accum loss scaling or clipping per-microbatch silently changes the effective learning rate and destabilizes the run.

notes.title: Concept - Scaling Laws
notes.scope: The power-law relationship of pretraining loss to compute, parameters, and data, and the compute-optimal allocation. IN: Kaplan vs Chinchilla, the L(N,D) form, IsoFLOP method, 20 tokens/param, the 6ND FLOP budget, inference-optimal overtraining. OUT: the repeated-data regime (link Concept - Data-Constrained Scaling Laws), emergent-abilities debate (link 18).
key_points: Loss model L(N,D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta with Chinchilla fits alpha~0.34, beta~0.28; training compute approximated as C ~ 6ND FLOPs (2 for the matmul, x3 for fwd+bwd, per param per token).

Kaplan et al. 2020 over-weighted parameters because the LR schedule was not re-tuned per run; Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) used IsoFLOP profiles plus a parametric fit and found N and D should scale roughly equally -> ~20 tokens/param at compute-optimal.
Gopher (280B params / 300B tokens) was badly undertrained; Chinchilla (70B / 1.4T) matched it with 4x fewer params at equal compute — the result that reset the field's param/token intuition.
Inference-optimal overtraining: Llama-3 8B on 15T tokens is ~1875 tokens/param, far past Chinchilla, deliberately trading extra training cost for a smaller/cheaper-to-serve model.
How to budget a run: from a compute number C, solve 6ND = C under the optimal N/D ratio (or your overtraining target) to get params and tokens, then wall-clock from tokens/sec.

Failure modes: extrapolating a fitted law outside its compute range; forgetting the constants depend on architecture/tokenizer/data; conflating pretraining-loss improvement with downstream benchmark gains (the loss is smooth, capabilities are not).
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run

notes.title: Concept - Data Parallelism and ZeRO
notes.scope: Replicated-model data parallelism and the ZeRO family that shards optimizer states, gradients, and parameters to cut per-GPU memory. IN: DDP all-reduce, ZeRO stages 1/2/3, communication volume per stage, offload. OUT: PyTorch FSDP as a distinct implementation (link Concept - Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)), all-reduce internals (link 08).
key_points: Plain DDP keeps a full model replica per rank, all-reduces gradients (ring algorithm), and steps the optimizer locally; memory per GPU stays at full model+grad+optimizer, so DDP alone adds throughput but not capacity.

ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2019, DeepSpeed): Stage 1 shards optimizer states across N ranks (/N), Stage 2 also shards gradients, Stage 3 also shards parameters (gathered just-in-time per layer during fwd/bwd), driving per-GPU state toward (model+grad+opt)/N.

Communication: ZeRO-1/2 keep all-reduce volume ~= DDP; ZeRO-3 replaces it with all-gather of params (each fwd and bwd) plus reduce-scatter of grads, ~1.5x DDP comm volume — the memory-for-bandwidth trade.
ZeRO-Offload / Infinity push optimizer states and params to CPU DRAM or NVMe, buying capacity at severe bandwidth cost (useful for fitting a model on few GPUs, not for max throughput).
Numbers: Adam optimizer state = 12 bytes/param (fp32 master + m + v); a 70B model's ~1.1TB of states sharded across 64 ranks is ~18GB/GPU under ZeRO-3.

Failure modes: comm becomes the bottleneck on slow interconnect; ZeRO-3 param-gather stalls the pipeline if not overlapped with compute; bucket sizing and prefetch depth need tuning to hide the all-gather latency.
links: Concept - Why Models Don't Fit on One GPU

notes.title: Concept - Tensor and Pipeline Parallelism
notes.scope: Intra-layer tensor parallelism (Megatron column/row split) and inter-layer pipeline parallelism (GPipe, 1F1B, interleaved), plus the pipeline bubble. IN: the TP all-reduce structure, PP schedules and bubble math, bandwidth vs latency sensitivity. OUT: sequence/context/expert parallelism (own notes), collective internals (link 08).
key_points: Tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al. 2019, Megatron-LM): the MLP is split column-parallel (first matmul) then row-parallel (second), so each block needs exactly one all-reduce in the forward and one in the backward; attention splits heads across ranks. TP comm rides on activations every layer, demands NVLink, and is usually kept <= 8 (within a node).
Pipeline parallelism partitions layers into stages; microbatches flow through, creating a fill/drain bubble of fraction (p-1)/(m+p-1) for p stages and m microbatches.

1F1B (PipeDream) interleaves one-forward-one-backward to cap activation memory; interleaved/virtual pipeline (Megatron) assigns multiple non-contiguous stages per device to shrink the bubble; zero-bubble and DeepSeek's DualPipe overlap further.

The core trade: TP has cheap-to-express but bandwidth-heavy activation all-reduces (fast link required), while PP has cheap point-to-point activation passes but pays the bubble and load-imbalance tax.

Numbers: large runs commonly use TP=8 with PP=8-16; raise microbatch count m >= ~4x pipeline depth to amortize the bubble; the last PP stage carries the loss/unembedding and the first carries embeddings, creating stage imbalance.

Failure modes: TP over a slow inter-node link collapses MFU; PP stage imbalance from embedding/loss layers; 1F1B still needs activation recomputation to fit long sequences; naive GPipe wastes memory storing all microbatch activations.
links: Concept - Multi-Head Attention Variants (MHA MQA GQA MLA)

notes.title: Concept - Mixed Precision Training
notes.scope: Training in reduced precision: bf16 vs fp16, fp32 master weights, loss scaling, and which ops stay in fp32. IN: the two 16-bit formats and their ranges, dynamic loss scaling, master-weight update, fp32-only ops, reduce dtype. OUT: fp8 training (link Concept - FP8 Training), float-format fundamentals (link 01 Concept - Floating Point for Deep Learning).
key_points: fp16 has 5 exponent bits (range ~6e-5 to 65504) and underflows small gradients, so it needs loss scaling: multiply loss by S before backward, unscale before the step; a dynamic scaler halves S on inf/nan and grows it periodically.

bf16 has 8 exponent bits (fp32's dynamic range) but only 7 mantissa bits; it needs no loss scaling but is coarser, which is why modern LLM pretraining is almost universally bf16 and fp16 has largely disappeared from pretraining.

Master weights: the optimizer keeps an fp32 copy because accumulating tiny updates directly into bf16 weights loses them to swamping (the update rounds away); compute in bf16, accumulate/update in fp32.

Ops kept in fp32 for stability: the loss, softmax, layernorm/rmsnorm statistics, attention-softmax accumulation, and gradient reductions; matmuls run in bf16 on tensor cores. TF32 is a middle ground for nominally-fp32 matmuls.
Numbers: ~2x activation memory saving and ~2-8x tensor-core throughput vs fp32 on A100/H100; the all-reduce accumulation dtype matters — reducing in bf16 loses precision at scale, so reduce in fp32.

Failure modes: fp16 loss-scale collapse (repeated overflow drives S->0, halting progress); bf16 precision causing slow silent divergence in very deep or very long runs; running layernorm in bf16 rather than fp32 causing instability.
links: Concept - Floating Point for Deep Learning
Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining
notes.scope: The LR schedule shapes used in LLM pretraining and their hyperparameters. IN: warmup, cosine decay, warmup-stable-decay (WSD/trapezoidal), inverse-sqrt, peak/min-LR and warmup-length choices, annealing on quality data. OUT: optimizer internals (link Concept - AdamW at Scale), LR/batch coupling (link Concept - Critical Batch Size), muP LR transfer (link Concept - muP and Hyperparameter Transfer).
key_points: Warmup: a linear ramp over ~0.5-4% of steps (often ~2000) while Adam's second-moment estimate is still uncalibrated; too short gives an early loss spike, too long wastes compute.
Cosine decay to ~10% of peak over the planned token budget; it requires knowing total steps in advance, and stopping early leaves you at a high LR with an artificially high loss.

WSD / trapezoidal (MiniCPM, Hu et al. 2024): warmup -> long constant phase -> short (10-20%) rapid decay; it matches cosine's final loss but lets you branch or continue from the stable phase and add data without recomputing the schedule.
The rapid decay phase is where much of the capability lands, and annealing on higher-quality or domain data during that phase (a data schedule) is now standard.
Peak-LR magnitudes: ~3e-4 for mid-size models, GPT-3 175B used 6e-5 with a huge batch; LR scales down with model width (muP) and up with batch size (roughly sqrt for Adam).

Failure modes: LR too high past warmup -> spikes/divergence; decaying to 0 vs 10% (10% often better for continued training); resuming a cosine run with the wrong remaining-steps count silently mis-schedules the rest of the run.
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run
Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Concept - AdamW at Scale
notes.scope: The engineering of AdamW for LLM pretraining. IN: decoupled weight decay, beta/epsilon choices at scale, fused/foreach kernels, sharded optimizer state, global-norm gradient clipping, param-group exclusions. OUT: the base Adam update rule (link 02 Concept - Adam and AdamW), second-order methods (link Concept - Second-Order Optimizers at Scale), Muon (link Concept - Muon Optimizer).
key_points: Decoupled weight decay (Loshchilov & Hutter 2017): AdamW applies decay directly to weights (theta -= lr*wd*theta) rather than folding it into the gradient, so decay strength is independent of the adaptive per-parameter scaling; typical wd = 0.1.

Betas at scale: beta1=0.9 with beta2=0.95 (not 0.999) is near-universal LLM folklore — a lower beta2 tracks the gradient-variance estimate faster and reduces spike sensitivity; GPT-3, OPT, and PaLM all use beta2~0.95. Epsilon 1e-8 is standard, with occasional 1e-15 experiments.
Memory: Adam stores fp32 m and v (8 bytes) plus the fp32 master weight (4 bytes) = 12 bytes/param; this is exactly the state ZeRO/FSDP shard, and it dominates footprint in low-activation regimes.

Engineering: fused or foreach kernels apply the update across all params in one launch; gradient clipping by global norm (usually 1.0); skip the step entirely on non-finite grads; separate param groups so weight decay is excluded from norms, biases, and often embeddings.
Failure modes: applying weight decay to layernorm gains/embeddings hurts; epsilon swamping in bf16; missing gradient clipping invites spikes; unsharded optimizer state OOMs at scale.

Non-obvious: excluding 1D parameters (norms, biases) from weight decay is standard but rarely written down; the beta2 choice, warmup length, and clip threshold together govern early-training stability.
links: Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining
Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Concept - Pretraining Objectives
notes.scope: The self-supervised objectives used to pretrain language models. IN: causal LM, masked LM, span corruption (T5), UL2, prefix-LM, and fill-in-the-middle (FIM), with their sample-efficiency tradeoffs and packing pitfalls. OUT: cross-entropy math (link 01 Concept - Entropy and Cross-Entropy), data mixing/ordering (link 05), post-training objectives (link 06).
key_points: Causal LM: predict token t+1 from tokens <= t with teacher forcing and cross-entropy over the vocab; every position contributes a loss (dense signal), which is why decoder-only CLM won at scale.
Masked LM (BERT, Devlin et al. 2018) masks ~15% of tokens and predicts them bidirectionally — good for representations but ~7x less loss signal per sequence than CLM and not natively generative.
Span corruption (T5, Raffel et al. 2020) masks contiguous spans and predicts them with sentinel tokens in an encoder-decoder; UL2 (Tay et al. 2022) mixes R/S/X denoisers selected by a mode token.

Fill-in-the-middle (Bavarian et al. 2022): reorder a document into prefix/suffix/middle with sentinel tokens so a causal LM learns infilling (essential for code completion); PSM vs SPM formats, FIM rate ~50-90% with negligible AR-loss cost.
Prefix-LM sits between CLM and MLM by allowing bidirectional attention over the prompt region while remaining causal on the continuation.

Failure modes: FIM format mismatch between training and inference; document packing bleeding attention across concatenated docs (needs reset masks or EOS separators); computing loss over padding tokens; sentinel tokens not reserved in the tokenizer.
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run

notes.title: Concept - Tokenizer Training
notes.scope: Choosing and training a tokenizer for pretraining. IN: BPE vs unigram LM (SentencePiece), vocab-size tradeoffs, normalization/pre-tokenization, digit and whitespace handling, multilingual fertility, reserved special tokens. OUT: the BPE merge algorithm itself (link Concept - Byte-Pair Encoding), inference-time failure arcana (link Gotchas - Tokenizers).
key_points: Unigram LM (Kudo 2018, SentencePiece): start from a large candidate set and iteratively prune by EM to maximize corpus likelihood; it is probabilistic and supports subword regularization (sampling segmentations), unlike greedy BPE.

Vocab-size tradeoff: a larger vocab shortens sequences (cheaper compute per document) but enlarges the embedding+softmax matrix (vocab x hidden params and the output-softmax FLOPs) and leaves rare tokens undertrained; common points are 32k (Llama-2), 128k (GPT-4, Llama-3), and 256k (Gemma).
Fertility (tokens per word) is the quality metric; multilingual and code corpora need larger vocab to keep fertility low, and English-centric tokenizers impose a 2-4x token tax on other languages.

Normalization (NFKC), byte fallback, and pre-tokenization matter: whether digits are split individually (Llama) or grouped up to three (GPT-4) changes arithmetic behavior; reserve slots for chat-template and FIM sentinel tokens up front.
Numbers: a 128k vocab x 4096 hidden embedding is ~512M params (often tied input/output); tokenizers are trained on a representative multi-GB sample, not the full corpus.

Failure modes: undertrained rare tokens become glitch tokens (link 18); adding tokens after pretraining without embedding resize/retraining; digit grouping hurting math; a normalization mismatch between training and serving.

notes.title: Concept - MoE Training and Load Balancing
notes.scope: The training dynamics unique to Mixture-of-Experts models. IN: top-k routing, auxiliary load-balance loss, router z-loss, aux-loss-free bias balancing, expert capacity and token dropping. OUT: MoE as an architecture (link 03 Concept - Mixture of Experts Architecture), the all-to-all comm mechanics (link Concept - Expert Parallelism).
key_points: Top-k routing (GShard, Lepikhin et al. 2020; Switch, Fedus et al. 2021) sends each token to k experts; without balancing pressure the router collapses onto a few experts, starving the rest.

Auxiliary load-balance loss penalizes the product of the fraction of tokens routed to an expert and that expert's mean router probability (Switch's L_aux, coefficient ~0.01); a router z-loss penalizes large router logits for numerical stability.

Aux-loss-free balancing (DeepSeek-V2/V3, 2024) adds a per-expert bias to the routing logits, adjusted by a feedback controller toward equal load, avoiding the auxiliary-loss gradient that fights the LM objective — DeepSeek reports lower loss at equal balance.

Expert capacity factor (1.0-2.0) sets a per-expert token buffer; overflow tokens are dropped (skip the expert, pass through the residual), trading capacity memory against dropped-token quality; dropless implementations (MegaBlocks) use grouped GEMM instead.
Numbers: DeepSeek-V3 uses 256 routed + 1 shared expert, top-8, 671B total / 37B active; fine-grained experts plus shared-expert isolation; upcycling converts a dense checkpoint into an MoE init.

Failure modes: expert collapse, router instability without z-loss, silent quality loss from capacity drops, straggler experts stalling the all-to-all in expert parallelism, and an aux-loss coefficient set too high (hurts LM loss) or too low (imbalance).
links: Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Reference - Parallelism Strategies
notes.scope: A lookup matrix of the parallelism dimensions used in distributed training. IN: for each of DP, ZeRO/FSDP, TP, PP, SP, CP, EP — what it shards, its collective/comm pattern, interconnect sensitivity, memory effect, typical degree, and primary failure mode. OUT: mechanistic explanations (own concept notes), collective-op internals (link 08).
key_points: One row per strategy with columns: what it splits (params / grads / optimizer / activations / experts / sequence), collective used (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all, point-to-point), comm volume per step, interconnect need (NVLink vs InfiniBand), memory reduction, typical degree, and failure mode.

DP/DDP: replicate model, all-reduce grads, no memory relief. TP: split within layer, all-reduce activations, NVLink-bound, degree <= 8. PP: split across layers, p2p activations, bubble cost. ZeRO-3/FSDP: shard states, all-gather + reduce-scatter, ~1.5x DDP comm.

SP: shard the norm/dropout/residual region along sequence to cut activation memory, complements TP at no extra comm volume. CP: shard the sequence for attention via ring/all-gather (long-context). EP: shard experts, two all-to-all collectives per MoE layer.
Placement rule-of-thumb: TP within a node, PP and DP across nodes, EP orthogonal on the expert dimension, CP for long context; degrees multiply to the world size (world = DP x TP x PP x CP x EP).
Footnotes: comm volume in bytes/step per layer; TP costs 2x(fwd+bwd) activation all-reduce per layer; ZeRO-3 ~= 1.5x DDP volume; all-to-all is latency- and topology-sensitive.
Date-stamp: reflects 2026 practice across Megatron-Core, DeepSpeed, PyTorch FSDP2, and TorchTitan.

notes.title: Snippet - Training a BPE Tokenizer
notes.scope: Runnable HuggingFace tokenizers code to train a byte-level BPE tokenizer with pre-tokenization, reserved special tokens, and individual-digit splitting, then verify the encode/decode round-trip and fertility. OUT: the BPE algorithm theory (link Concept - Byte-Pair Encoding) and vocab-size reasoning (link Concept - Tokenizer Training).
key_points: Use the tokenizers library: a ByteLevel pre-tokenizer (add_prefix_space=True), a BpeTrainer with vocab_size, min_frequency, and special_tokens ([BOS], [EOS], [PAD], plus FIM sentinels), and a ByteLevel decoder.
Add a Split rule to isolate digits into single tokens, and show the GPT-2 regex as the alternative pre-tokenization pattern.
Demonstrate the encode round-trip, measure fertility (tokens/word) on a held-out sample, and save/load tokenizer.json.

Why-it's-written: byte-level guarantees no UNK token; special and sentinel token IDs must be reserved up front because adding them later forces an embedding resize; add_prefix_space must match between training and inference; train on a representative sample, not the whole corpus.
Expected output: printed vocab size, a sample tokenization showing the space marker glyph and single-digit tokens, and a fertility number to sanity-check the vocab choice.

notes.title: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run
notes.scope: The end-to-end lifecycle of a large pretraining run, integrating the domain's owned mechanisms. IN: sizing from a compute budget, parallelism layout, the at-scale training loop, monitoring and intervention, failure/restart handling, and annealing to release. OUT: data-pipeline construction (link 05) and cluster provisioning (link 08); this note links rather than re-derives owned mechanisms.
key_points: Sizing: from a compute budget C (GPU-hours x FLOPs/GPU x MFU) derive the 6ND token/param split via Chinchilla or an overtraining target, then estimate wall-clock from tokens/sec = batch_tokens / step_time and total cost.

Parallelism layout: pick DP x TP x PP x (EP/CP) for the model and cluster, then set microbatch and grad-accum to hit a target global batch (e.g., 4M tokens); target MFU 40-55% and distinguish MFU from HFU (hardware FLOPs utilization inflated by recompute).

The loop: a resumable, packed-sequence dataloader; forward/backward with activation recompute; global-norm clip; optimizer step; gradient all-reduce; and logging of loss, grad-norm, LR, tokens-seen, and MFU, with async checkpoints every N steps.

Monitoring and intervention: watch for loss spikes and grad-norm blowups and apply the rewind/skip-batches/lower-LR recovery; at 10k+ GPUs a node fails every few hours, so elastic restart from checkpoint is routine, not exceptional.

Architecture/walkthrough diagram (Mermaid): budget -> config -> warmup -> stable -> decay/anneal -> eval -> release. Evolution: GPT-3 -> PaLM -> Chinchilla-optimal -> inference-optimal overtraining (Llama-3) -> fp8 MoE (DeepSeek-V3).

Numbers: Llama-3 405B trained on ~16k H100s for ~54 days over ~15T tokens in bf16 with 4D parallelism; DeepSeek-V3 in ~2.788M H800 hours in fp8. Failure modes: a bad data shard triggering a spike, checkpoint corruption, silent gradient desync, non-determinism defeating reproducibility.
links: Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining
Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Concept - Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)
notes.scope: PyTorch FSDP/FSDP2 internals and how they realize ZeRO-3-style sharding. IN: the all-gather/reduce-scatter unit, FlatParameter vs per-parameter DTensor sharding, wrapping policy, prefetch/overlap, mixed-precision and offload knobs, and differences from DeepSpeed ZeRO-3. OUT: the ZeRO algorithm itself (link Concept - Data Parallelism and ZeRO), collective internals (link 08).
key_points: FSDP shards params/grads/optimizer across the DP group (equivalent to ZeRO-3): it all-gathers a unit's full params just before its fwd/bwd, frees them after, and reduce-scatters grads afterward; the unit granularity is set by the wrapping policy (typically per transformer block).

FSDP1 uses a FlatParameter (a unit's params concatenated into one flat tensor), which complicates per-parameter LR, optimizer groups, and state dicts; FSDP2 uses per-parameter DTensor sharding — cleaner, composable with TP via DeviceMesh — and is the 2024-2025 migration path used by TorchTitan.
Overlap is what makes it fast: prefetch the next unit's all-gather during the current unit's compute (forward and backward prefetch), tuned with backward_prefetch and limit_all_gathers.

Config knobs: MixedPrecisionPolicy (param/reduce/buffer dtypes — reduce in fp32!), sharding_strategy (FULL_SHARD, SHARD_GRAD_OP ~= ZeRO-2, HYBRID_SHARD for shard-within-node/replicate-across), CPUOffload, and composition with activation checkpointing.

Numbers: HYBRID_SHARD cuts inter-node comm by keeping the shard within a node and replicating across nodes; wrapping the whole model as one FSDP unit defeats overlap and peaks at full-model memory (a common anti-pattern).

Failure modes: wrong wrapping granularity (too coarse OOMs or kills overlap, too fine adds comm overhead); a bf16 reduce dtype losing gradient precision at scale; sharded state-dict pitfalls; combining with TP requiring a 2D device mesh.

notes.title: Concept - Sequence and Context Parallelism
notes.scope: Two sequence-dimension parallelism techniques for training. IN: Megatron sequence parallelism (sharding the norm/dropout region to save activation memory, paired with TP) and context parallelism (ring/all-gather attention that shards the sequence for long-context training), plus causal load balancing. OUT: ring attention as a serving/kernel technique (link 08/18), attention math (link 03).
key_points: Megatron sequence parallelism (Korthikanti et al. 2022): the regions TP leaves replicated (layernorm, dropout, residual add) are sharded along the sequence, converting the TP all-reduce into all-gather + reduce-scatter and cutting activation memory by ~the TP degree with no added comm volume — the standard companion to TP.

Context parallelism shards the sequence across CP ranks; because each query must attend to all keys, ring attention (Liu et al. 2023) passes KV blocks around a ring, overlapping the communication with the block-wise attention compute (or all-gathers KV directly).
Causal load balancing: a naive contiguous sequence split makes later ranks do more attention work under the causal mask, so zigzag/striped token assignment rebalances the per-rank cost.

Numbers: unfused attention activation memory scales ~O(seq^2) per layer, which CP (and FlashAttention's block-wise recompute) tames; CP degree multiplies the trainable context length toward 100k-1M tokens.
CP composes with FlashAttention (both are block-wise online-softmax) and with TP/SP, but the device-mesh ordering matters.

Failure modes: CP communication becoming the bottleneck when not overlapped; causal load imbalance; correctness bugs in the online-softmax rescaling across ring steps; RoPE position bookkeeping across shards.

notes.title: Concept - Expert Parallelism
notes.scope: Distributing MoE experts across devices and the all-to-all communication it requires. IN: the dispatch/combine all-to-all, all-to-all bottlenecks and node-limited routing, load imbalance and stragglers, composition with other parallelism dimensions. OUT: MoE architecture (link 03) and the load-balancing losses (link Concept - MoE Training and Load Balancing).
key_points: Expert parallelism places different experts on different GPUs; each MoE layer needs two all-to-all collectives — dispatch tokens to their expert's device and combine the results back — with comm volume proportional to tokens x hidden x top-k.

All-to-all is latency- and bandwidth-sensitive, and cross-node all-to-all over InfiniBand is the dominant MoE overhead; DeepSeek-V3 caps it with node-limited routing (a token's experts span <= M nodes) plus DualPipe overlap and custom communication kernels.

Load imbalance creates stragglers: an overloaded expert's device stalls the all-to-all barrier for everyone, so capacity dropping bounds worst-case load and couples training-time balance directly to systems efficiency.

Composition: EP is orthogonal to DP/TP/PP and is often combined as EP x DP over the expert dimension; grouped GEMM / MegaBlocks enables dropless expert compute; the all-to-all should be overlapped with the expert GEMM.
Numbers: DeepSeek-V3 (671B total / 37B active, 1 shared + 8-of-256 routed) runs EP across many GPUs with all-to-all consuming a meaningful fraction of step time.
Failure modes: all-to-all hangs/deadlocks, straggler stalls from imbalance, silent token dropping under capacity, EP+PP scheduling interactions, and NCCL all-to-all tuning on the specific fabric.
links: Concept - MoE Training and Load Balancing

notes.title: Pattern - 3D Parallelism Composition
notes.scope: How to compose DP x TP x PP (and EP/CP) into a coherent device layout. IN: the world-size factorization, placement/ordering rules mapped to physical topology, DeviceMesh, memory/comm reasoning, and microbatch interaction. OUT: each dimension's internal mechanism (own concept notes); this is the composition design pattern.
key_points: Problem: no single parallelism scales alone — DP hits a memory wall, TP hits the interconnect, PP hits the bubble — so the pattern factors world = DP x TP x PP x CP x EP and maps each factor onto the hardware topology.

Placement forces: TP needs the fastest link (NVLink, intra-node, degree <= 8); PP tolerates slow links (point-to-point activations, inter-node); DP is outermost (all-reduce, bandwidth-tolerant with overlap); CP handles long sequences; EP is orthogonal on the expert dimension.

DeviceMesh (PyTorch/Megatron): assign ranks so TP groups are intra-node, then compute per-GPU memory ~= sharded_states/(DP*shard) + activations/(TP*CP*PP), and set microbatch count m >= ~4x pipeline depth to amortize the bubble.
Known uses: Megatron-LM (Narayanan et al. 2021, 'Efficient Large-Scale LM Training on GPU Clusters'), DeepSpeed 3D, TorchTitan (FSDP2 + TP + PP), and DeepSeek-V3 (DP + EP + PP DualPipe).

Tradeoffs: more TP lowers per-GPU memory but raises comm and drops MFU past a node boundary; more PP is comm-cheap but adds bubble and activation memory; the search is a small grid guided by these rules, not brute force.
Failure modes: TP spanning nodes (MFU collapse), too few microbatches (huge bubble), mesh ordering mismatched to the fabric, and forgetting activation memory in the per-GPU budget.

notes.title: Concept - Critical Batch Size
notes.scope: The gradient-noise-scale theory of batch size and its consequences for LLM pretraining. IN: the noise scale, diminishing returns past the critical batch, LR/batch coupling, batch-size ramping, the compute-vs-wall-clock Pareto. OUT: gradient-accumulation mechanics (link Concept - Gradient Accumulation and Microbatching), LR schedule shapes (link Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining).
key_points: The gradient noise scale B_noise ~= tr(H*Sigma)/(g^T H g) (approximated in practice via the ratio of gradient variance to gradient magnitude) marks where larger batches stop buying linear step-count speedups.

McCandlish, Kaplan et al. 2018 ('An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training'): the critical batch grows during training (as the loss falls, the noise scale rises), so late training tolerates larger batches — motivating batch-size warmup (GPT-3 ramped from 32k to 3.2M tokens).

LR/batch coupling: the linear scaling rule holds for small batches, while Adam at large batch scales roughly as sqrt; the peak LR must track the batch size or the extra samples are wasted (or the run diverges).
Numbers: GPT-3's final batch was 3.2M tokens, PaLM ~1-4M; below the critical batch you are compute-efficient but slow, above it you are fast but burning compute for little per-step gain.

Failure modes: running far above the critical batch to fill a large cluster wastes compute (a common utilization trap); running far below it starves MFU; ramping the batch too fast triggers early instability.
Non-obvious: the 'right' batch depends on whether you optimize wall-clock or total compute, and the critical batch is a moving target you can deliberately exploit with a batch-size schedule.
links: Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining
Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run

notes.title: Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes
notes.scope: The mechanisms behind pretraining instabilities and the interventions that tame them. IN: spike anatomy, qk-norm, embedding/logit control, beta2/LR/clip levers, precision effects, and the rewind-skip-lower-LR recovery. OUT: z-loss/soft-cap output tricks in depth (link Concept - z-loss and Logit Soft-Capping), the war stories (link Lore - The Loss Spike Chronicles), float-format basics (link 01).
key_points: Spike anatomy: the gradient norm blows up, the loss jumps, and the run either self-recovers or diverges; spikes correlate with attention-logit growth, layernorm-gain growth, and occasionally a specific data batch.

Known stabilizers: qk-layernorm (normalize Q and K before attention — Dehghani et al. 2023 ViT-22B, OLMo-2), z-loss on the output softmax (PaLM, coeff ~1e-4), embedding-LR/embedding-norm control, lower beta2 (0.95), tighter gradient clipping, and pre-norm/residual-scaling choices.

Root causes: bf16 rounding accumulation over depth, attention entropy collapse (logits grow, softmax saturates), dead or exploding experts in MoE, garbage/repeated data, too-high LR after warmup, and un-normalized embeddings.
Recovery playbook: rewind to a pre-spike checkpoint, skip the offending data batches, temporarily lower the LR, then resume — the recipe used across OPT-175B, PaLM, and GLM-130B.
Numbers: spikes grow more frequent at larger scale and lower precision; GLM-130B used embedding-gradient shrink; PaLM documented ~20 spikes and the skip-batches-on-restart fix.

Failure modes: distinguishing a sharp optimizer/data spike from slow bf16 divergence, and from a hardware ECC/NaN masquerading as an optimization spike; over-clipping can hide a real data problem instead of fixing it.
links: Playbook - Debugging a Diverging Training Run
Concept - MoE Training and Load Balancing

notes.title: Concept - Distributed Checkpointing
notes.scope: Saving and loading sharded model+optimizer state at scale. IN: sharded vs consolidated checkpoints, asynchronous checkpointing, full resumability (RNG/dataloader), reshard-on-load, and the checkpoint-interval math. OUT: the parallelism that produces the shards (own notes), storage hardware (link 08).
key_points: The problem: a 405B run's fp32 optimizer state is multiple TB, so each rank saves only its own shard (torch.distributed.checkpoint / DCP, or Megatron/DeepSpeed formats); consolidating shards into a single file is a separate offline step.

Async checkpointing copies state to pinned CPU memory and writes it in a background thread, so training stalls for seconds rather than minutes; DCP's async_save overlaps the write with subsequent compute.

Resumability needs more than weights: optimizer moments, the LR-scheduler step, the dataloader position and shuffle seed, RNG states, and tokens-seen — omitting any produces a discontinuity spike or re-exposes data.
Reshard-on-load: loading a TP=8/PP=16 checkpoint into a different mesh (for continued pretraining or fine-tuning) requires resharding, which DTensor/DCP handle but naive flat checkpoints do not.

Numbers: the optimal checkpoint interval balances write cost against lost work on failure (Young/Daly: interval ~= sqrt(2 * MTBF * checkpoint_time)); at 16k GPUs with failures every few hours this drives frequent checkpoints.

Failure modes: a corrupted/partial checkpoint from a crash mid-write (needs atomic rename plus keep-last-N), missing RNG/dataloader state, OOM during consolidation, and slow storage bottlenecking the entire cluster during a save.
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run
Checklist - Pre-Launch for a Large Training Run

notes.title: Concept - FP8 Training
notes.scope: Training in 8-bit floating point. IN: the E4M3/E5M2 formats, per-tensor/per-block scaling, delayed scaling, which tensors stay high-precision, fp32 accumulation, and the DeepSeek-V3 fine-grained recipe. OUT: fp8 for inference/quantization (link 07), float-format fundamentals (link 01), tensor-core hardware (link 08).
key_points: Formats (Micikevicius et al. 2022, OCP FP8): E4M3 (more mantissa, range ~+/-448) for forward activations/weights and E5M2 (more range) for gradients; Hopper/Blackwell tensor cores run fp8 matmuls ~2x faster than bf16.

Scaling is everything because fp8's dynamic range is tiny: per-tensor scale factors, with delayed scaling (reuse an amax history from prior steps) vs current-tensor amax; DeepSeek-V3 uses fine-grained per-tile (1x128) and per-block (128x128) scaling to bound quantization error.

What stays high precision: fp32 master weights and optimizer states, layernorm, and softmax; critically, the fp8 matmul must accumulate in fp32 — Hopper tensor cores accumulate at reduced precision, so DeepSeek added an fp32 accumulation path via CUDA cores.

Numbers: DeepSeek-V3 was the first production-scale fp8-pretrained LLM (~2.788M H800 hours), running most GEMMs in fp8 with sensitive parts in bf16/fp32 and reaching near-bf16 loss with large throughput and memory wins.

Failure modes: an amax spike blowing the scale (overflow/underflow), reduced-precision accumulation error compounding over depth, sensitive layers (embeddings, output, first/last blocks) needing bf16, and calibration drift between the forward and backward passes.
Non-obvious: fp8 pretraining was folklore-unstable until per-block scaling plus fp32 accumulation made it production-viable in 2024-2025, and it is now the frontier cost default.
links: Concept - Floating Point for Deep Learning
Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Decision - Choosing a Parallelism Strategy
notes.scope: A framework for picking parallelism degrees given model size, GPU count/HBM, interconnect, and context length. IN: the default decision flow, the inputs that drive it, a tradeoff matrix with numbers, flip conditions, and worked examples. OUT: the mechanics of each strategy (own concept notes) and the memory formulas (link 08 Reference).
key_points: Default (80% case): if the model+states fit in one node, use FSDP/ZeRO alone; if too big for a node, add TP within the node (degree <= 8) plus FSDP across nodes; for very deep models on many nodes, add PP; for MoE add EP; for long context add CP.
Decision inputs: model params and optimizer bytes vs total HBM; intra- vs inter-node bandwidth (NVLink ~900 GB/s vs InfiniBand ~400 Gb/s); sequence length; dense vs MoE; and the GPU count.

Tradeoff matrix (strategy x memory-saved, comm-cost, MFU-impact, complexity) with numbers: TP kills MFU past a node boundary, PP adds bubble, ZeRO-3/FSDP adds ~1.5x comm, CP is for sequences beyond ~32k.

Flip conditions: a slow interconnect argues against TP (prefer PP + ZeRO); abundant NVLink (GB200 NVL72) makes higher TP viable; a tiny cluster may need ZeRO-Offload; inference-latency-driven shape choices differ from training-optimal ones.
Worked examples: 7B on 8xH100 (FSDP); 70B on 64 GPUs (FSDP + TP8); 405B on 16k (DP + TP8 + PP16 + SP); 671B MoE (DP + EP + PP DualPipe).
Failure modes: over-parallelizing a model that already fits (needless comm), placing TP across nodes, ignoring activation memory in the budget, and leaving no headroom for allocator fragmentation.
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run

notes.title: Breakdown - Megatron-LM
notes.scope: How NVIDIA's Megatron-LM implements large-scale transformer training and set the throughput standard. IN: its tensor parallelism (f/g operators), sequence parallelism, selective recompute, interleaved pipeline, and fused kernels. OUT: general parallelism theory (own concept notes); this reverse-engineers the specific framework.
key_points: Headline: Narayanan et al. 2021 demonstrated ~1T-parameter training at ~52% MFU on 3072 A100s; Megatron-Core is the de-facto reference many labs fork.

Tensor parallelism design: column-parallel then row-parallel linears so each transformer block needs exactly two all-reduces in forward and two in backward, expressed as the conjugate f and g operators (f = identity fwd / all-reduce bwd, g = all-reduce fwd / identity bwd); attention is split by heads.

Sequence parallelism (Korthikanti et al. 2022) shards the TP-replicated norm/dropout regions along sequence to cut activation memory; selective activation recomputation recomputes only the attention block (the cheap-to-recompute, memory-heavy part) rather than everything.

The interleaved (virtual) pipeline schedule assigns multiple non-contiguous stages per device to shrink the bubble; a ZeRO-1-style distributed optimizer shards Adam state; PP point-to-point overlaps with DP all-reduce.
Clever parts: fused kernels (bias+GeLU, scaled masked softmax), the exact selective-recompute policy, the mesh mapping that keeps TP intra-node, and gradient-accumulation fusion.

What's dated / what to steal: FlatParameter-style sharding is being superseded by DTensor/FSDP2, but the f/g operator design, selective recomputation, and interleaved schedule remain the things to steal.
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run

notes.title: Snippet - FSDP Minimal Setup
notes.scope: A minimal runnable PyTorch FSDP2 (fully_shard) training step with per-block wrapping, mixed precision (bf16 compute, fp32 reduce), and activation checkpointing. OUT: FSDP internals (link Concept - Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)) and multi-node launch/topology (link 08).
key_points: Show fully_shard (FSDP2) applied per transformer block and then to the root module, a MixedPrecisionPolicy(param_dtype=bf16, reduce_dtype=fp32), and a DeviceMesh for the DP dimension.
Include the training step (forward, loss, backward, optimizer.step) noting that FSDP handles all-gather/reduce-scatter transparently, plus the torchrun launch line.
Wrap blocks with checkpoint_wrapper for activation checkpointing and note the compute-for-memory trade.

Why-it's-written: wrap per block (not the whole model) so all-gather overlaps compute; reduce in fp32 to avoid gradient-precision loss at scale; apply sharding before torch.compile; save with DCP (sharded) rather than a full state_dict.
Expected output: per-step loss decreasing on a toy batch and ~1/N peak memory versus a single-GPU baseline.

notes.title: Checklist - Pre-Launch for a Large Training Run
notes.scope: The pre-flight verification before committing thousands of GPU-hours. IN: config/sizing sanity, numerics, data, checkpoint/restart, observability, and a short canary run. OUT: the run-time debugging procedure (link Playbook - Debugging a Diverging Training Run).
key_points: Config/sizing group: token budget vs Chinchilla/overtraining target; global-batch and grad-accum arithmetic; LR-schedule total steps match the token budget; parallelism degrees multiply to world size; weight decay excluded from norms and embeddings.
Numerics group: bf16 vs fp8 decision made; reduce dtype fp32; loss/softmax/norm computed in fp32; gradient clip set; z-loss/qk-norm enabled if the architecture/history warrants.
Data group: shards enumerated and shuffled; packing/attention-reset masks verified; no eval-set contamination (link 13); dataloader resumable; BOS/EOS/pad handling checked.
Checkpoint/restart group: async checkpoint tested; a restart-from-checkpoint reproduces the loss exactly (RNG + dataloader state restored); atomic write with keep-last-N retention.
Observability group: loss/grad-norm/LR/MFU/tokens-seen dashboards; NaN/inf alerts; per-rank health; ETA and cost tracking.

Canary: run 500-2000 steps at the target config, confirm the MFU target (40-55%), no spike, and that checkpoint+resume works, before scaling up. Each 'why' item ties to a real incident (wrong remaining-steps on resume, a contaminated shard, a bf16-reduce divergence).
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run
Playbook - Debugging a Diverging Training Run
Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Gotchas - Distributed Training
notes.scope: The pitfalls of multi-GPU/multi-node training, ordered by pain. IN: NCCL hangs from collective mismatch, silent gradient desync, non-determinism, uneven data shards, and rank/mesh/env misconfiguration. OUT: single-GPU numeric issues (link Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes) and collective internals (link 08).
key_points: NCCL hang on collective mismatch: one rank takes a data-dependent code path and issues a different number of collectives, so the job hangs until timeout. Detection: NCCL_DEBUG, the collated watchdog, and TORCH_NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING; fix: make control flow rank-invariant.

Silent gradient desync: a subtle bug (different dropout seed, an unsynced buffer, a missed all-reduce) lets ranks drift apart while training appears fine. Detection: periodically all-reduce a parameter checksum and assert equality.

Non-determinism: per-rank dataloader worker seeding, nondeterministic cuDNN kernels, and atomic reductions break reproducibility; deterministic mode plus per-rank seeded RNG fixes it at a throughput cost.
Uneven shards / last batch: unequal samples per rank deadlock DDP when one rank finishes early; use drop_last or the Join context, and DistributedSampler.set_epoch for correct reshuffling.
Rank/mesh/env misconfig: wrong WORLD_SIZE/RANK/LOCAL_RANK/MASTER_ADDR, a TP group that is not intra-node (silent MFU collapse), or mismatched CUDA/NCCL versions across nodes.
Each gotcha follows symptom -> cause -> fix -> detection, with hangs listed first because they burn the most wall-clock before anyone notices.
links: Playbook - Debugging a Diverging Training Run

notes.title: Concept - muP and Hyperparameter Transfer
notes.scope: Maximal Update Parametrization (muP) and hyperparameter transfer from a small proxy to a large target. IN: the width-invariance the parametrization enforces, the specific scaling rules, the coordinate check, muTransfer in practice, depth-transfer caveats. OUT: standard init/LR (link 02), scaling laws for loss (link Concept - Scaling Laws).
key_points: The problem muP solves: under standard parametrization the optimal LR shifts with model width, forcing a re-tune per size; muP makes activations and updates width-invariant so the LR (and other HPs) transfer unchanged.

Mechanism (Yang & Hu 2021, 'Tensor Programs V'): scale initialization variance and per-layer LR by fan-in factors, use 1/width attention-logit scaling (instead of 1/sqrt(d)), and scale output logits by 1/width; input, hidden, and output layers get different treatments.
Coordinate check: verify that activation coordinate magnitudes stay O(1) across widths at init and after a few steps — the empirical test that a muP implementation is correct.

In practice (muTransfer): tune LR/betas/init on a narrow proxy (e.g., width 256) and transfer to the full model; used by Cerebras-GPT and MiniCPM publicly, and reportedly for GPT-4-scale HP search, saving enormous tuning compute.
Numbers: LRs that transfer across 10-100x width; the specific multipliers (embedding LR, 1/d attention scaling); width transfer is solid, depth transfer is newer and shakier (depth-muP).

Failure modes: a partial/incorrect muP (some rules applied, not all) is worse than none; a silently failing coordinate check; interactions with weight decay and warmup; and schedules/depth that do not transfer.
links: Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining

notes.title: Concept - Data-Constrained Scaling Laws
notes.scope: Scaling when unique data runs out. IN: repeating data (multi-epoch value decay), the reformulated law with a repetition-decay term, and the params-vs-repeats tradeoff under a fixed data budget. OUT: the compute-optimal Chinchilla law (link Concept - Scaling Laws), data curation/mixing (link 05).
key_points: Muennighoff et al. 2023 ('Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models'): repeating data up to ~4 epochs is nearly as valuable as fresh data; beyond ~4 epochs the marginal value decays fast, and by ~16 epochs added repeats are near-worthless.

The law is reformulated with a decay term so repeated tokens count as an effective data volume below their nominal count; when data-bound, extra compute is better spent on parameters than on more repeats.
Practical levers under a data limit: repeat (<= ~4 epochs), add code/synthetic data (link 05), spend compute on params, or up-weight scarce high-quality data during the LR-decay phase.
Numbers: Chinchilla's 20 tokens/param assumes unique data; frontier runs at 15T+ tokens are exhausting high-quality web text, so repetition plus synthetic data are increasingly necessary as of 2026.

Failure modes: over-repeating drives memorization/overfitting and benchmark-contamination risk (link 13); conflating tokens-seen with unique-tokens; and repetition interacting badly with weak deduplication (link 05).
Non-obvious: this is the mechanistic reason the field pivoted to synthetic data and aggressive dedup — the data wall, not compute, is the binding constraint for frontier pretraining.
links: Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run

notes.title: Concept - Muon Optimizer
notes.scope: The Muon optimizer: orthogonalizing momentum updates via Newton-Schulz iteration for 2D parameters. IN: the mechanism, why it helps, the Newton-Schulz coefficients and LR coupling, and its scale-up (Moonlight/Kimi). OUT: Adam/AdamW (link Concept - AdamW at Scale, 02) and other second-order methods (link Concept - Second-Order Optimizers at Scale).
key_points: Mechanism (Jordan et al. 2024): for 2D weight matrices, take the momentum buffer and replace it with its nearest orthogonal matrix via a few Newton-Schulz iterations (approximating UV^T from the SVD), giving spectral-norm-controlled updates; embeddings, norms, and 1D params still use AdamW.
Why it works: it equalizes the update magnitude across singular directions (a cheap whitening/Shampoo-like effect) without storing a preconditioner, reporting ~2x compute-efficiency at small scale.

Practical details: it couples to weight decay and a per-matrix LR, needs a scale adjustment relative to AdamW's LR, uses quintic Newton-Schulz coefficients with ~5 iterations, and handles non-square matrices by orienting the iteration.
Numbers: Moonlight (Kimi, ~16B MoE, 2025) trained at scale with Muon, reporting ~2x token-efficiency and memory savings versus Adam (no second-moment buffer for 2D params, just momentum).

Failure modes: applying Muon to embeddings/output/1D params (breaks it), wrong LR scaling versus AdamW, Newton-Schulz instability from too few iterations or bad input scaling, and distributed orthogonalization across sharded matrices.
Non-obvious: Muon is a 2024-2025 frontier result still being validated at true frontier scale — promising, not yet the settled default; watch for scale-up caveats.
links: Concept - Matrix Multiplication as the Atom of Deep Learning
Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining

notes.title: Concept - Second-Order Optimizers at Scale
notes.scope: Preconditioned and sign-based optimizers for LLM training. IN: Shampoo/distributed Shampoo, SOAP, and Lion — their preconditioners/updates, memory and compute cost, and where they beat AdamW. OUT: AdamW engineering (link Concept - AdamW at Scale), Muon specifically (link Concept - Muon Optimizer).
key_points: Shampoo (Gupta et al. 2018): a per-layer Kronecker-factored preconditioner (left L and right R factors for a weight matrix) with update L^(-1/4) G R^(-1/4), capturing curvature Adam ignores; distributed Shampoo (Anil et al. 2020) amortizes the inverse-root across steps and shards the factors.
SOAP (Vyas et al. 2024) runs Adam inside Shampoo's eigenbasis, combining Shampoo's preconditioner with Adam's cheap per-step update and fewer hyperparameters, competitive on wall-clock.

Lion (Chen et al. 2023, found by symbolic search): the sign of an interpolated momentum, so it stores one buffer (half of Adam's state), but needs a smaller LR (~3-10x) and larger weight decay; it sometimes matches AdamW and sometimes underperforms at scale.

Cost/benefit: Shampoo's preconditioner matmuls and inverse-roots add ~10-40% overhead plus extra memory (L, R per layer) but can cut steps-to-target — it won an MLCommons AlgoPerf training-algorithm track and is used in some Google production runs.
Numbers: the preconditioner is refreshed only every ~100+ steps, large matrices are blocked, and the eigh/inverse-root cost is the main overhead; Lion's memory is half of Adam's.
Failure modes: Shampoo numerical issues in the inverse-root (needs fp32/damping), block-size vs accuracy tradeoffs, Lion's LR/wd retuning (a naive Adam LR diverges), and stale preconditioners.
links: Concept - Matrix Multiplication as the Atom of Deep Learning
Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes

notes.title: Breakdown - DeepSeek-V3 Training
notes.scope: How DeepSeek-V3 was trained so cheaply. IN: fp8 pretraining, aux-loss-free MoE, DualPipe, Multi-Token Prediction, and the co-designed systems stack. OUT: MoE architecture generalities (link 03) and inference-time MLA/serving (link 07).
key_points: Headline: 671B total / 37B active MoE, 14.8T tokens, ~2.788M H800 GPU-hours (~$5.6M in compute) at near-frontier quality — the efficiency shock of late 2024.

FP8 training: fine-grained per-tile and per-block scaling plus fp32 accumulation via CUDA cores (working around Hopper's reduced-precision tensor-core accumulation), with most GEMMs in fp8 and sensitive parts in bf16/fp32.

Aux-loss-free load balancing: a per-expert bias adjusted by a controller instead of an auxiliary loss that fights the LM objective, plus a small sequence-wise balance term; 256 routed + 1 shared expert, top-8, with node-limited routing.

DualPipe: a bidirectional pipeline schedule that overlaps forward and backward across the pipeline to nearly eliminate the bubble and overlaps all-to-all EP communication with compute, using custom low-level communication kernels.

Multi-Token Prediction (MTP): auxiliary heads predict several future tokens during training for a denser signal and better representations, and the same heads enable speculative decoding at inference.

What to steal / what's dated: the fp8 recipe, aux-loss-free routing, and hardware-co-designed comm; caveats are that the H800's constrained interconnect shaped the design and reproducibility leans on their infra tricks.
links: Concept - MoE Training and Load Balancing
Concept - Multi-Head Attention Variants (MHA MQA GQA MLA)
Deep Dive - Anatomy of a Pretraining Run

notes.title: Snippet - muP Coordinate Check
notes.scope: Runnable code that verifies a muP implementation by measuring activation coordinate magnitudes across model widths at init and after a few steps. OUT: the muP theory itself (link Concept - muP and Hyperparameter Transfer).
key_points: Build the same model at several widths (e.g., 128/256/512/1024), apply muP scaling (init variance, per-layer LR, output multiplier), and run a few optimizer steps on a fixed batch and seed.
Record the mean absolute activation per layer per width; a correct muP keeps these ~constant across width (flat lines), while standard parametrization shows systematic growth or shrinkage with width.

Why-it's-written: the coordinate check is the only reliable catch for a broken muP (a single wrong multiplier passes unit tests but fails here); measure at step 0 and step ~5 (both matter); hold data and seed identical across widths so width is the only variable.
Expected output: a table or plot where muP curves overlap across widths and standard-parametrization curves fan out, giving a clear pass/fail read on the implementation.
links: Concept - Learning Rate Schedules for Pretraining

notes.title: Gotchas - Tokenizers
notes.scope: Tokenizer pitfalls that silently corrupt training and eval, ordered by pain. IN: add-token/embedding-resize traps, train/inference normalization drift, double-BOS, digit handling, undertrained/glitch tokens, and encoding non-invertibility. OUT: glitch-token phenomenology (link 18 Lore - Glitch Tokens) and the training procedure (link Concept - Tokenizer Training).
key_points: Add-token trap: appending special tokens after pretraining without resizing and initializing the embedding + unembedding (and retraining) yields garbage logits or index errors, because the new tokens have random embeddings the model never learned.

Train/inference normalization drift: a mismatch in NFKC, whitespace, or add_prefix_space between tokenizer training and serving silently re-tokenizes text and degrades quality; the classic double-BOS bug is a chat template and the tokenizer both prepending BOS.
Digit tokenization: grouping digits (GPT-4 groups up to three) versus splitting them (Llama, single digits) changes arithmetic ability, and left-to-right vs right-to-left chunking creates artifacts.

Undertrained/glitch tokens: tokens present in the vocab but nearly absent from training data (e.g., scraped usernames like ' SolidGoldMagikarp') keep near-random embeddings and trigger bizarre behavior; detect with an embedding-norm histogram (link 18).

Encoding edge cases: byte-level round-trips on invalid UTF-8, a partial multibyte sequence at a truncation boundary, and trailing-whitespace merges; changing the tokenizer silently invalidates prior eval comparisons.
Each gotcha follows symptom -> cause -> fix -> detection (e.g., assert re-encode(decode(x)) == x as a round-trip guard).

notes.title: Lore - The Loss Spike Chronicles
notes.scope: The war stories of pretraining instabilities across public runs and the folklore fixes they produced. IN: OPT-175B, PaLM, GLM-130B, and BLOOM spike accounts, the recover-and-skip recipe, and the mechanistic lesson. OUT: the stabilizer mechanisms in depth (link Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes) and the OPT logbook as history (link 19 Lore - The OPT-175B Logbook).
key_points: OPT-175B (Zhang et al. 2022): the logbook's litany of hardware failures, loss divergences, LR lowerings, and fp16 loss-scale battles — the canonical honest account; here the focus is the spike-and-recover tactics, with the fuller history linked to 19.

PaLM (Chowdhery et al. 2022): ~20 loss spikes where no single bad batch was the culprit — restarting ~100 steps before the spike and skipping those batches avoided it, yet the same data trained fine later, showing spikes are an optimizer-state x data interaction, not just 'bad data'.

GLM-130B (Zeng et al. 2022): attributed instability to embedding-layer gradient growth and attention-softmax blow-up, and fixed it with embedding-gradient shrink and DeepNorm; it also documented fp16-vs-bf16 pain on non-NVIDIA hardware.

BLOOM / Megatron folklore: the 'restart, skip, lower LR' recipe entered common practice, and bf16 was adopted specifically to escape fp16 loss-scale collapse; qk-norm and z-loss became standard because of these episodes.

The mechanical lesson: a spike is where the second-moment estimate is stale relative to a sudden gradient direction, so lowering beta2, clipping, warmup, and skipping the batch each address a different part — the field's stabilizers are scar tissue from these runs.
Evidence status: the OPT logbook is verified/published; the PaLM and GLM accounts are well-sourced from their papers; the exact folklore recipes are well-sourced practitioner lore.

notes.title: Playbook - Debugging a Diverging Training Run
notes.scope: The operational procedure when a live run's loss spikes, diverges, or NaNs. IN: triage, isolating data vs optimizer vs hardware vs numerics, and the recover-or-restart decision. OUT: the underlying stabilizer mechanisms (link Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes).
key_points: Step 1 triage: classify the event — a sharp spike (optimizer/data), slow drift (numerics/bf16), or a NaN at a specific step (hardware ECC / bad tensor) — by reading grad-norm, loss, and per-rank health first.

Step 2 isolate data: replay the suspected batch from a clean checkpoint; if it does not reproduce (as PaLM found), it is an optimizer-state interaction; if it does, inspect the batch for repeated tokens, garbage docs, or an encoding bug.

Step 3 isolate hardware/numerics: a single-rank NaN implicates a GPU (ECC or silent data corruption), while an all-rank event implicates optimization; verify the reduce dtype is fp32 and layernorm runs in fp32.

Step 4 recover: rewind to a pre-spike checkpoint, skip N offending batches, optionally lower the LR temporarily, tighten the grad clip, or enable z-loss + qk-norm, then resume — with the expected observation for each action.

Step 5 escalate: on repeated spikes, apply a structural fix (lower peak LR, lower beta2, add stabilizers) and consider precision (move sensitive layers fp8->bf16); decide when to kill and re-launch versus babysit.
A branch table maps symptom -> likely cause -> fix jump; verification is that the loss rejoins its pre-spike trajectory within M steps.

notes.title: Reference - LLM Pretraining Hyperparameters
notes.scope: A sourced lookup table of the actual hyperparameters real frontier runs used, with the folklore constants surfaced. IN: peak/min LR, warmup, token batch, betas/eps, weight decay, grad clip, precision, optimizer, vocab, tokens/param across GPT-3, Chinchilla, PaLM, OPT, Llama-1/2/3, DeepSeek-V3, and more. OUT: the reasoning behind each choice (link the optimizer/LR/precision concept notes).
key_points: Rows are models; columns are params, tokens, tokens/param, peak LR, min LR, warmup (steps/tokens), global batch (tokens), beta1, beta2, epsilon, weight decay, grad clip, precision, optimizer, and vocab size — date-stamped and sourced per row.

Folklore constants surfaced: beta2 = 0.95 (GPT-3/OPT/PaLM) rather than 0.999; wd = 0.1; grad clip = 1.0; warmup ~0.1-2% of steps; min LR = 10% of peak; no weight decay on norms/embeddings; z-loss coeff ~1e-4.
The overtraining trend across rows: Chinchilla ~20 tokens/param -> Llama-3 8B ~1875 tokens/param (inference-optimal overtraining), and GPT-3's batch-size ramp from 32k to 3.2M tokens.
The precision column tracks the fp16 -> bf16 -> fp8 migration over 2020-2025; the optimizer column shows AdamW dominance with Muon and Shampoo as frontier experiments.
Footnotes clarify units (tokens vs sequences, peak vs constant LR, warmup in steps vs tokens) and mark 'undisclosed' where labs did not publish, keeping the table honest.
Every cell is labeled published vs folklore per the quality contract, so a reader knows what is verified versus practitioner lore.

notes.title: Concept - z-loss and Logit Soft-Capping
notes.scope: The output-stabilization tricks that keep pre-softmax logits numerically well-conditioned. IN: z-loss (penalizing the log-partition function), final-logit and attention-logit soft-capping, the qk-norm relation, and the models that use each. OUT: broad loss-spike causes/recovery (link Concept - Training Stability and Loss Spikes), softmax basics (link 02).
key_points: z-loss (PaLM, Chowdhery et al. 2022): add alpha * (log Z)^2 where Z = sum(exp(logits)) is the softmax normalizer, pushing log Z toward 0 so the denominator stays ~1; this prevents logit blow-up and improves bf16 stability, with alpha ~1e-4, and reappears as router z-loss in MoE.
Logit soft-capping (Gemma 2): bound final logits as cap * tanh(logits / cap) (cap ~30) and attention logits (cap ~50) so no single logit dominates — a bounded complement/alternative to z-loss.

Mechanism: unbounded logits saturate the softmax, which vanishes the gradient and overflows exp in fp16/bf16; z-loss and capping keep the pre-softmax distribution in a numerically safe, well-conditioned range.

QK-norm relation: normalizing Q and K before attention (qk-layernorm, used by OLMo-2 and ViT-22B) bounds attention logits structurally, an alternative to attention-logit capping — the design space is 'how to keep logits bounded'.

Numbers: z-loss coeff ~1e-4 to 1e-3; soft-cap 30/50; the real tradeoff is throughput — soft-capping breaks FlashAttention's fast path, which is why Gemma 2 later dropped attention soft-capping for kernel compatibility.

Failure modes: a z-loss coeff set too high over-regularizes and hurts LM loss, soft-capping is incompatible with fused attention kernels, and capping can mask a deeper LR/data instability rather than fix it.
